newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco companies challenge proposed Mass. law.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco companies challenge proposed Mass. law.

text.p: The lawyers for top tobacco companies said Friday they feared losing invaluable trade secrets should a Massachusetts law forcing the disclosure cigarette and smokeless tobacco ingredients be enacted.

Henry Dinger, arguing before a federal court that the Massachusetts law should be blocked, said it would reveal to competitors the "flavorings" which give individual cigarette brands their particular tastes. "It is axiomatic that the public disclosure of those ingredients anywhere would destroy those trade secrets everywhere," Dinger told the court.

The law, scheduled to go into effect July 1, would make Massachusetts the first state to require tobacco companies to disclose their ingredients to a state agency. It would also set tougher tests to measure the nicotine intake from cigarettes, snuff and chewing tobacco.

The four cigarette companies challenging the law -- Philip Morris Cos Inc. ; R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp ; Brown & Williamson Tobacco Co, a unit of B.A.T Industries Plc ; and Lorillard Tobacco Co, a unit fo Loews Corp -- account for about 90 percent of the cigarettes sold in the state.
The six smokeless tobacco companies suing the state include United States Tobacco, a unit of UST Inc, and Brown & Williamson.
Dinger said the Massachusetts law would preempt federal laws governing the tobacco industry, which require ingredients to be submitted to the U.S. Department of Health and kept confidential.
"Congress sought to protect the confidentiality of the ingredient list. Massachusetts proposes to disclose it. The two statutes cannot be squared," Dinger said.

However, assistant attorney general Rebecca McIntyre, representing Massachusetts, said the federal law only covers the marketing and advertising of tobacco, and Congress did not expressly bar the states from making their own laws.
"Both the federal and the state statutes permit the disclosure of ingredient information under certain conditions," McIntyre said.

If the law were passed, Massachusetts would examine the ingredient list and release to the public those ingredients which it believes could cause health problems, said Gregory Connolly, a director with the state public health department.
The tobacco companies have threatened in court papers to stop selling in Massachusetts if the law were passed.
Mass. Sen. Warren Tolman, who sponsored the legislation, said a dozen states have contacted him about the proposed law and are closely monitoring the court case.
"We expect that similiar legislation will be filed in at least half a dozen states," he told Reuters following the court case.
Judge George O'Toole told the court he would take the matter under advisement. McIntyre said it may take as long as six weeks to two months before a decision is made.
